html:
Punch-marked coins are the earliest coins of India: small, irregular pieces of silver, and sometimes copper, stamped with several separate symbols by punches. They date from about the 6th century BCE to the 2nd century BCE.

They appeared in the Ganges plain in the age of the Mahajanapadas, the "great realms", when towns and trade grew and the Buddha and Mahavira were teaching. They came about the same time as, and perhaps independently of, the first coins in Lydia in western Anatolia.

The symbols include suns, wheels, hills, trees, animals and the six-armed sign; their meaning is not certain, but some may mark the issuing authority. A common standard was the silver karshapana of about 3.4 grams.

When Magadha grew into the Maurya Empire, its punch-marked coins spread across most of the subcontinent and set a common money. They stayed in use long after, until struck coins with names and portraits, such as those of the Indo-Greeks and Kushans, took over.
sum: Punch-marked coins are the earliest coins of India: small, irregular pieces of silver, and sometimes copper, stamped with several separate symbols by punches. They date from about the 6th century BCE to the 2nd century BCE.
